## Choose the model feature you want to check

A model can estimate a plausible mean curve while missing other patterns in
the data. Counts can vary more than their fitted distribution allows. Residuals
from successive measurements can remain correlated. Differences between groups
can show up as extra variation around the mean curve. {gratia} provides
residual diagnostics and posterior predictive checks to investigate these
patterns in GAMs, linear models and mixed models.

We check the response distribution, variation between groups and dependence
between observations made in sequence.
[Model diagnostics for distributional, discrete and censored responses](response-distributions.html)
extends the examples to distributional parameters, censoring and weights.
The articles on [`mgcv::gfam()`](gfam-support.html),
[{glmmTMB}](glmmTMB-support.html) and [{sdmTMB}](sdmTMB-support.html) illustrate
diagnostics for those model classes.

These examples require gratia 0.12.0 or later, R >= 4.4.0 and {mgcv} >= 1.9-4.
We load mgcv and gratia for fitting and diagnostics, and {dplyr} and {ggplot2} for
working with the results. The growth
example also needs the optional {nlme}, {lme4} and {gamm4} packages (gamm4 >= 0.2-7).
The plot examples use 50 replicated datasets to keep them quick to run. Use
more draws and check that the plots are stable before interpreting small
departures in the tails.

```{r packages}
library("gratia")
load_mgcv()
library("dplyr")
library("ggplot2")
```

There are three distinct ways to generate a comparison:

| Question | Calculation | What varies between simulated datasets? |
|---|---|---|
| Is the variation around the fitted values typical for this model? | Conditional response simulation or QQ reference | Responses vary around the same fitted effects. |
| Can the model reproduce these features of the data once we allow for uncertainty in the fitted effects? | Conditional posterior predictive check | Each dataset uses a new draw of the fitted effects as well as new responses. |
| How much variation should we expect among new groups or spatial fields? | Marginal response simulation or marginal posterior predictive check | New group or field effects are drawn from their fitted distribution. A posterior predictive check can also draw uncertain parameters, depending on the model. |

A smooth plot's interval concerns an estimated effect. A QQ reference band
concerns ordered residuals from replicated responses. A posterior predictive
plot concerns replicated response distributions. QQ reference bands condition
on the fitted model, without refitting it for each replicate. Use departures
from these bands to locate discrepancies to investigate, rather than as a
formal rejection rule.

Plot subtitles identify the method. Short captions identify conditioning,
field choices, joint simulation bands or omitted bands. Routine pointwise bands
are unlabelled. Posterior predictive captions identify conditioning only.
Use `caption = ""` to omit a caption
or supply your own text. Scalable QQ and worm plots use the same labels as their
ordinary counterparts.

## Check the response distribution and the mean of count data

Consider daily insect counts at independently sampled sites. We simulate
12,000 sites with temperature and wind as covariates. The mean count peaks at
intermediate temperatures and falls with wind. Conditional on these covariates,
each count follows a Poisson distribution.

```{r counts-data}
set.seed(301)
insects <- data.frame(temperature = runif(12000, 5, 30),
  wind = runif(12000, 0, 10))
insects$count <- rpois(nrow(insects),
  exp(2.5 - ((insects$temperature - 19) / 8)^2 - 0.1 * insects$wind))
```

We fit a smooth temperature effect and a linear wind effect to recover these
relationships:

```{r counts}
count_fit <- bam(count ~ s(temperature, bs = "cr", k = 12) + wind,
  data = insects, family = poisson(), method = "fREML", discrete = TRUE)
```

The simulation uses Poisson counts, whose variance equals their mean at
fixed temperature and wind. We use quantile residuals to check the fitted
response distribution and look for remaining patterns in the mean or spread.
In real data, counts can vary more than a Poisson model predicts, in which
case a negative binomial model may fit better.

```{r count-appraisal, fig.height=7}
appraise(count_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 302)
```

With 10,000 or more observations used in the fit, `appraise()` switches to
scalable plots that summarise all observations in bins. This makes the
distribution easier to see when many points would overlap. A roughly
straight QQ plot and similar residual spread across fitted values are
consistent with the Poisson model. The observed-versus-fitted panel
shows the amount of variation around the fitted means.

### Calculate PIT and quantile residuals

A probability integral transform (PIT) residual describes an observation's
position in its fitted response distribution. For a count $y$ with fitted
cumulative distribution function (CDF) $F$, it is a random draw between
$F(y-1)$ and $F(y)$. Quantile residuals apply the
standard-normal quantile function to that probability. This randomisation
avoids artificial steps caused by integer responses. For continuous outcomes
the probability is simply $F(y)$. We calculate both residual types for the same
observations and seed to show how the probability becomes a normal score:

```{r count-probabilities}
u <- quantile_residuals(count_fit, type = "pit", seed = 302)
r <- quantile_residuals(count_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 302)
head(data.frame(observed = insects$count, fitted = fitted(count_fit),
  probability = u, normal_score = r))
```

These probabilities should be roughly uniform between zero and one if the
model describes the response distribution well. Their quantile residuals
should then be approximately standard normal. Poisson deviance residuals have
a different distribution, so we simulate reference quantiles from the fitted
model for their QQ plot.

```{r count-reference, fig.height=4.5}
qq_plot(count_fit, type = "deviance", method = "simulate",
  n_simulate = 50, seed = 303)
```

Here the reference comes from responses simulated at the fitting covariates.
Each observation's fitted mean enters its simulated response.
`method = "uniform"` simulates responses by applying the fitted inverse CDF to
randomly shuffled uniform quantiles, then averages the ordered residuals
across replicates.
`method = NULL` chooses this method for most independent GAMs. For Tweedie
models it uses simulation from the fitted family because evaluating their
inverse CDF is costly. You can choose a method explicitly where supported.
A worm plot subtracts reference quantiles from the ordered residuals. This
makes small departures easier to see as patterns around zero. Here we use
quantile residuals and summarise the QQ curve in 80 bins:

```{r count-worm}
scalable_worm_plot(count_fit, type = "quantile", qq_bins = 80, seed = 302)
```

### Look for what the QQ plot could miss

A response distribution can look plausible when observations are pooled while
systematic lack of fit remains at some covariate values. Remove the curved
relationship to temperature to see this:

```{r omitted-curve}
linear_fit <- glm(count ~ temperature + wind, data = insects,
  family = poisson())
scalable_residuals_covariate_plot(linear_fit,
  covariates = c("temperature", "wind"), type = "pearson")
```

The curved residual mean against temperature shows where the linear effect
misses the response shape. Response residuals subtract the fitted mean from
the count. Pearson residuals then divide that difference by its fitted standard
deviation. For a broader distributional check, use `type = "quantile"` or
`type = "pit"` to examine location, spread and tails against each covariate.
For non-Gaussian deviance residuals, a mean away from zero can occur even when
the model fits well.

The ordinary and scalable covariate plots default to `smooth = NULL`, which fits the residual mean trend
only for groups with at most 20,000 eligible observations. Use `smooth = TRUE`
to fit trends for larger groups, or `smooth = FALSE` to omit them. The threshold
is applied separately within each response, family component and `by` group.

The ordinary version shows individual residuals. It is useful for smaller
teaching examples; both versions use all eligible observations:

```{r ordinary-covariates}
small_insects <- insects[seq_len(500), ]
small_fit <- gam(count ~ temperature + wind, data = small_insects,
  family = poisson(), method = "REML")
residuals_covariate_plot(small_fit, covariates = "temperature", type = "pearson")
```

By default each distinct model covariate gets one panel. To select covariates
through a smooth, supply its exact label from `smooths(count_fit)`:

```{r smooth-covariates}
smooths(count_fit)
scalable_residuals_covariate_plot(count_fit, terms = "s(temperature)",
  type = "quantile", seed = 302)
```

For tensor products use labels such as `"te(temperature,wind)"`, without adding
spaces. `terms` accepts smooth labels only, while `covariates` can also select
covariates fitted as linear terms or covariates absent from the model. Supply the original
fitting `data` for omitted covariates or when raw transformed covariates are
unavailable. For a categorical covariate, the functions show residual boxplots
and group means; `by = "group"` separates patterns into group facets.

Separate panels can miss a remaining interaction. Here the mean contains a
product of two independent, centred covariates, plus independent Gaussian
errors with standard deviation one. Averaging over either covariate hides the
interaction in the other covariate's residual mean:

```{r omitted-interaction-data}
set.seed(306)
interaction_data <- data.frame(x = runif(4000, -1, 1), z = runif(4000, -1, 1))
interaction_data$y <- 4 * interaction_data$x * interaction_data$z + rnorm(4000)
```

We deliberately omit the interaction from this model, then compare separate
residual plots with a map of the residuals over both covariates:

```{r omitted-interaction, fig.height=5}
additive_fit <- gam(y ~ s(x) + s(z), data = interaction_data, method = "REML")
scalable_residuals_covariate_plot(additive_fit, covariates = c("x", "z"),
  pairs = list(c("x", "z")), bins = c(10, 10), type = "pearson")
```

The map shows the mean residual within each occupied cell. Opposite corners
have residuals of the same sign, with the two diagonals differing in sign.
This is the pattern expected here when the model omits the interaction.
Cells with fewer than `min_n`
observations are blank. Use `statistic = "sd"` to inspect changes in spread
instead; this is particularly useful with quantile or PIT residuals. Correlated
covariates can share residual patterns, so check a revised model before
attributing the pattern to one particular effect. If a smooth reaches its
basis dimension limit, try increasing `k` and check whether that reduces the
residual pattern in the refitted model.

### Use density and count summaries for large datasets

Scalable plots summarise the observations so dense regions remain readable.
The first two plots below compare smoothed densities with histogram bins;
the other two show observed versus fitted counts and the residual distribution:

```{r scalable-controls}
scalable_residuals_linpred_plot(count_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 302)
scalable_residuals_linpred_plot(count_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 302,
  density_method = "histogram")
scalable_observed_fitted_plot(count_fit)
scalable_residuals_hist_plot(count_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 302)
```

The default residual heatmap uses a kernel estimate of density at each predictor
value. Its square-root colour scale keeps low-density regions visible. The
histogram option uses unsmoothed bins; `bandwidth` controls smoothing on both
axes. Observed-versus-fitted count heatmaps remain unsmoothed. The scalable
functions also include `scalable_qq_plot()`; ordinary plots remain available
with `appraise(..., scalable = FALSE)`, and `scalable_threshold` changes the
automatic cutoff. Simulation still generates a response for every observation,
so using a compact display does not reduce the number of observations checked.

We can also compare the observed count distribution with replicated datasets.
This posterior predictive check includes coefficient uncertainty as well as
response variation:

```{r count-ppc}
posterior_predictive_plot(count_fit, n = 50, seed = 304, scalable = TRUE)
```

For each count, the plot compares its observed proportion with the median and
central 90% of its proportions in the replicated datasets. These intervals
describe variation across whole datasets. If there are more than 512 distinct
count values, the plot shows proportions in 512 labelled bins instead.
`appraise(ppcheck = TRUE, n_ppc = 50)` replaces the residual histogram with this
comparison. Offsets supplied as fitting arguments are retained in posterior
response draws. Explicit seeds preserve the caller's random-number state;
coefficient draws and response draws use separate streams.

## Repeated measurements: fixed effects, fitted groups and new groups

The Orthodont data contain dental measurements on 27 children at ages 8, 10,
12 and 14. Each child contributes several observations, so their values can
share an individual growth trajectory. A Gaussian linear mixed model with
sex-specific age slopes and correlated child intercepts and slopes is a useful
starting point. With only four occasions per child, very detailed individual
curves are not supported.

```{r growth-fit}
library("nlme")
library("lme4")
library("gamm4")
data("Orthodont", package = "nlme")
growth <- transform(Orthodont, age_c = age - 11)
growth_fit <- lme(distance ~ Sex * age_c, random = ~ age_c | Subject,
  data = growth, method = "REML")
summary(growth_fit)$tTable
```

The age coefficient describes mean growth in the reference sex, and the
interaction describes a difference in age slopes. The fitted random effects
describe departures for these children. The positive fitted age slopes
describe growth between ages 8 and 14. We now compare two questions: does the
model describe measurement variation around these children's fitted curves,
and does it describe the variation expected across new children?

```{r growth-references}
qq_plot(growth_fit, type = "quantile", conditioning = "conditional", seed = 305)
qq_plot(growth_fit, type = "quantile", conditioning = "marginal",
  n_simulate = 50, seed = 305)
```

The conditional comparison holds each child's fitted intercept and slope fixed
and checks remaining measurement variation. The marginal comparison generates
new child trajectories. All four simulated measurements for a child share a
new intercept and slope drawn together from their fitted distribution.
In this fit the conditional scores have a compressed centre and one large
positive tail departure. The marginal plot averages over different child
trajectories and is closer to its reference. Investigate the observation
responsible for the largest conditional score alongside that child's
trajectory.

The marginal QQ plot simulates complete sets of measurements to account for
the dependence among measurements from each child when it constructs its
reference bands.

The QQ plot pools the ordered residuals. To check the shared child effects,
also plot trajectories or residuals against age, grouped by child: systematic
patterns within children can be hidden by pooling.

Each panel below shows one child's quantile residuals against age centred at
11 years. Look for residuals that change systematically with age or remain
mostly on one side of zero. We omit a smoother because each child has only
four measurements.

```{r growth-within-child, fig.height=8}
residuals_covariate_plot(growth_fit, covariates = "age_c", by = "Subject",
  type = "quantile", conditioning = "conditional", smooth = FALSE, seed = 305,
  xlab = "Age relative to 11 years")
```

The following posterior predictive checks address the same conditional and
marginal questions while also allowing uncertainty in the estimated effects:

```{r growth-ppc}
posterior_predictive_plot(growth_fit, conditioning = "conditional", n = 50,
  seed = 306)
posterior_predictive_plot(growth_fit, conditioning = "marginal", n = 50,
  seed = 306)
```

The conditional posterior predictive check draws the fitted child effects
and fixed effects together, then simulates measurements around the sampled
growth curves. The marginal check draws new child effects from their fitted
population distribution each time it simulates measurements. Both nlme
calculations hold the covariance parameters at their fitted values. The
density overlays pool the measurements across ages and children. Use the
trajectory plots to examine where that variation occurs.

### Check models fitted with lme4 and gamm4

We first fit the same linear growth model with `lmer()` and check its
conditional quantile residuals. We then fit a shared smooth age curve with
`gamm4()`, retaining a separate intercept for each child, and inspect its
smooth and variance components:

```{r other-growth-fit}
growth_lmer <- lmer(distance ~ Sex * age_c + (age_c | Subject),
  data = growth, REML = TRUE)
appraise(growth_lmer, conditioning = "conditional", type = "quantile", seed = 305)
growth_smooth <- gamm4(distance ~ Sex + s(age, k = 4),
  random = ~(1 | Subject), data = growth)
draw(growth_smooth)
variance_comp(growth_smooth)
```

The direct `lmer()` fit answers the same linear-growth question. The `gamm4()`
fit instead asks whether a shared population age curve is curved, with child
intercepts accounting for repeated observations. It can be passed directly to
gratia. `draw()`, predictions, derivatives and fitted-value draws describe its
population GAM component; group terms specified in `random` are excluded from
those calculations. Variance components include both smooth penalties and
native group effects, with missing interval bounds where the fit provides none.
Next we check the complete mixed model and obtain predictions from the
population GAM component for girls aged 8 to 14:

```{r gamm4-checks}
appraise(growth_smooth, conditioning = "conditional", seed = 307)
posterior_predictive_plot(growth_smooth, n = 50, seed = 307)
population_grid <- data.frame(age = seq(8, 14, length.out = 30),
  Sex = factor("Female", levels = levels(growth$Sex)))
fitted_values(growth_smooth, data = population_grid) |> head()
```

Diagnostics and response simulations for `gamm4()` default to the full
conditional mixed model, including fitted child and smooth effects. Posterior
response draws default to uncertainty in those fitted effects. Explicit
`conditioning = "gam_component"` selects the extracted GAM calculations, and
is required for posterior response draws at new data or supplied coefficient
draws. `conditioning = "marginal"` generates new mixed-model effects; for `gamm4()`
this includes the spline effects represented as random effects, so it asks a
different question from new measurement errors around a fixed age curve.
The existing `gamm()` response simulator still defaults to its GAM component;
request full-model conditioning explicitly there. See
[`gamm4_support`](../reference/gamm4_support.html) for covariance and sampling
restrictions. Use fitting-package prediction on the `mer` component for
predictions conditional on a particular child's effects.

## Check serial dependence in Gaussian and count models

The following simulation represents regularly spaced measurements from four
independent monitoring series with a slowly changing mean. The Gaussian
errors follow a first-order autoregressive (AR1) process, with a correlation
of 0.6 between successive errors in the same series. We pass this known
correlation as `rho` so `bam()` uses it during fitting. For your own data,
sort the rows by series and then by time within each series. Set `AR.start`
to `TRUE` at the first observation of each series. After fitting, we inspect
the QQ plot and look for correlation in the adjusted residuals.

```{r gaussian-series}
set.seed(308)
monitor <- expand.grid(time = seq_len(120), station = factor(seq_len(4)))
monitor$start <- monitor$time == 1
monitor$measurement <- 2 + sin(monitor$time / 25) +
  unlist(lapply(seq_len(4), function(i)
    as.numeric(arima.sim(list(ar = 0.6), n = 120, sd = 0.5))))
serial_fit <- bam(measurement ~ s(time, bs = "cr", k = 12), data = monitor,
  rho = 0.6, AR.start = start, discrete = TRUE)
qq_plot(serial_fit, method = "simulate", n_simulate = 50, seed = 309)
residual_correlation_plot(serial_fit, lag_max = 15)
residual_correlation(serial_fit, lag_max = 3)
```

For a Gaussian BAM with an identity link, the reference simulations preserve
the AR1 covariance and start an independent series at each `AR.start`. The
correlation plot uses residuals standardised by the supplied AR1 correlation to look
for remaining correlation. The companion table reports the correlation and
number of usable pairs at each lag, with fewer pairs at longer lags. Lags count
observation positions. With irregular measurements, equal lags can therefore
represent different lengths of time.

For counts, `bam()` with `discrete = TRUE` applies `rho` to its *working
residuals*, the quantities used during iterative fitting. This adjusts the
fit for correlation using a generalised estimating equations (GEE)
approximation. It leaves the joint distribution of the counts unspecified.
We illustrate this with Poisson counts whose log means depend on the
correlated Gaussian measurements simulated above.

```{r count-series-data}
set.seed(310)
monitor$count <- rpois(nrow(monitor), exp(1 + monitor$measurement / 2))
```

We fit a Poisson BAM with the working correlation correction, then inspect
its quantile residuals and the remaining correlation in its working residuals:

```{r count-series}
working_fit <- bam(count ~ s(time, bs = "cr", k = 12), data = monitor,
  family = poisson(), discrete = TRUE, rho = 0.6, AR.start = start)
qq_plot(working_fit, type = "quantile", seed = 311)
residual_correlation_plot(working_fit, type = "working.standardized", lag_max = 15)
```

The fitted Poisson probabilities still locate each count in its own response
distribution. The QQ plot omits bands because the working correlation does not
supply a joint distribution for the counts. For traditional residuals, the
default QQ reference pools the individual fitted residual distributions.
The correlation plot examines working residuals after adjusting for the fitted
AR1 correlation; this is an approximate check for remaining serial dependence.
`type = "standardized"` instead uses mgcv's stored `std.rsd`, which is not
necessarily the weighted working residual used during non-Gaussian fitting.
Here the large negative lag-one correlation after that adjustment suggests that
the supplied working correction is too strong. We supplied the latent
Gaussian correlation, whereas the correction acts on working residuals from
the count model. These correlations can differ. The upper-tail departure in
the QQ plot also reflects variation from the latent process that the Poisson
distribution omits. Use these two checks to examine the working correction
and the response distribution separately.

`qq_plot(working_fit, method = "simulate")`, joint `simulate()` and
`posterior_predictive_plot()` are explicitly unsupported. The same restriction
applies to nonidentity Gaussian and extended-family working AR1 BAM fits,
and to correlated non-Gaussian PQL `gamm()` fits. Approximate PQL checks without
residual working correlation remain available. A non-Gaussian mixed model
that specifies how observations depend on one another, for example through
AR1 effects on the log mean in glmmTMB, can provide joint predictive
simulations. That choice needs to reflect how dependence is thought to arise
in the data.

## Choose checks for the part of the model you want to examine

Use PIT or quantile checks for response distributions, predictor plots for
mean and variance structure, and ordered or spatial displays for dependence.
Conditional and marginal comparisons can disagree because they ask different
questions. The sdmTMB article develops four choices for fitted fields, including
one posterior field draw and integration over fitted-field uncertainty; these
are separate from simulating new fields or drawing parameter uncertainty.

[`diagnostic_support`](../reference/diagnostic_support.html) lists the precise
supported families and conditioning modes. Unsupported cases remain errors:
quasi families do not specify a full response distribution, censored posterior checks
need an observation mechanism, and a working correlation alone is insufficient
for a joint simulator. Models with independent responses use analytic
uniform/normal score references where available. Dependent responses use joint
simulation for bands where possible; otherwise the plot explains their omission.
